claim: The eukaryotic cell membrane is connected to a dense actin rich cortex.
source: The eukaryotic cell membrane is connected to a dense actin rich cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about eukaryotic cells.

claim: Dense membrane bound actin networks have severe influence on lipid phase separation.
source: We present FCS and STED experiments showing that dense membrane bound actin networks have severe influence on lipid phase separation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the FCS and STED experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Actin binding to ternary membranes prevented macroscopic liquid-ordered and liquid-disordered domain formation, even at low temperature.
source: In general, actin binding to ternary membranes prevented macroscopic liquid-ordered and liquid-disordered domain formation, even at low temperature.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the abstract.

claim: An actin correlated multi-domain pattern was observed depending on the type of pinning lipid.
source: Instead, depending on the type of pinning lipid, an actin correlated multi-domain pattern was observed.
evidence: This observation is reported from the experimental results in the abstract.

claim: FCS measurements revealed hindered diffusion of lipids in the presence of an actin network.
source: FCS measurements revealed hindered diffusion of lipids in the presence of an actin network.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: The lipid raft theory relates lipid phase separation to membrane protein partitioning and regulation.
source: The most prominent concept for membrane organization, the lipid raft theory, relates lipid phase separation (driven by interactions between cholesterol, sphingolipids, and saturated phospholipids) to membrane protein partitioning and regulation (Simons and Ikonen, 1997; Simons et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Simons and Ikonen, 1997 and Simons et al., 2011.

claim: Ternary model membranes containing two phospholipid species and cholesterol macroscopically phase separate into liquid-ordered and liquid-disordered domains at low temperature.
source: A convenient starting point is to envision the membrane as a two-dimensional (2D) fluid environment through which the various membrane components freely diffuse. This simple picture successfully captures ternary model membranes containing two phospholipid species and cholesterol. At low temperature, these systems macroscopically phase separate into liquid-ordered (Lo) and liquid-disordered (Ld) domains (Veatch and Keller, 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Veatch and Keller, 2003.

claim: The nature of the phase transition in ternary model membranes is consistent with that of a 2D fluid.
source: and the nature of the transition is consistent with that of a 2D fluid (Honerkamp-Smith et al., 2008, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Honerkamp-Smith et al., 2008, 2009.

claim: Similar phase separation behavior was observed in plasma membrane-derived vesicles.
source: Similar behavior was observed in plasma membrane-derived vesicles (Baumgart et al., 2007; Sezgin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baumgart et al., 2007 and Sezgin et al., 2012.

claim: Lo/Ld domains observed in model membranes grow macroscopic in size (micrometers).
source: For example, a remaining puzzle is that the Lo/Ld domains observed in model membranes grow macroscopic in size (micrometers), whereas lipid domains in plasma membrane are postulated to be tiny (nanometers) (Lenne and Nicolas, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lenne and Nicolas, 2009.

claim: Lipid domains in plasma membrane are postulated to be tiny (nanometers).
source: For example, a remaining puzzle is that the Lo/Ld domains observed in model membranes grow macroscopic in size (micrometers), whereas lipid domains in plasma membrane are postulated to be tiny (nanometers) (Lenne and Nicolas, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lenne and Nicolas, 2009.

claim: The temperature Tc below which Lo/Ld domains start to form in plasma membrane derived vesicles is distinctly below T = 37°C.
source: Additionally, the temperature Tc below which Lo/Ld domains start to form in plasma membrane derived vesicles is distinctly below T = 37°C (Sezgin et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sezgin et al., 2012.

claim: Lipid domains at temperatures above Tc can be induced by crosslinking low abundant membrane constituents.
source: In the case of a free-standing membrane (i.e., in the absence of an actin cortex), experiments have shown that lipid domains at temperatures above Tc can be induced by crosslinking low abundant membrane constituents (Hammond et al., 2005; Lingwood et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hammond et al., 2005 and Lingwood et al., 2008.

claim: The cortical cytoskeleton has been identified as a key player affecting membrane domain formation.
source: In addition to this, the cortical cytoskeleton has also been identified as a key player affecting membrane domain formation (Kusumi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kusumi et al., 2005.

claim: The cortical cytoskeleton is a dense fiber network of actin and spectrin on the cytoplasmic side of the eukaryotic plasma membrane.
source: The latter is a dense fiber network of actin and spectrin on the cytoplasmic side of the eukaryotic plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the cortical cytoskeleton.

claim: The cortical cytoskeleton network is connected to the membrane via pinning sites, such as lipid-binding proteins, transmembrane proteins, or membrane-attached proteins.
source: This network is connected to the membrane via pinning sites, such as lipid-binding proteins, transmembrane proteins, or membrane-attached proteins (Janmey, 1998; Mangeat et al., 1999; Janmey and Lindberg, 2004; Saarikangas et al., 2010 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Janmey, 1998; Mangeat et al., 1999; Janmey and Lindberg, 2004; Saarikangas et al., 2010.

claim: The picket-fence model proposes that the membrane is laterally compartmentalized by pinning sites that structure the membrane into small compartments whose perimeters are defined by the underlying actin network.
source: This has led to the hypothesis of the membrane being laterally compartmentalized: the pinning sites structure the membrane into small compartments whose perimeters are defined by the underlying actin network (the so-called 'picket-fence' model).
evidence: This describes the picket-fence model hypothesis.

claim: The picket-fence network acts as a barrier to diffusion, which accounts for confined diffusion of lipids and proteins observed in single molecule tracking experiments.
source: This picket-fence network then acts as a barrier to diffusion, which elegantly accounts for confined diffusion of lipids and proteins observed in a single molecule tracking experiments (Kusumi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kusumi et al., 2005.

claim: A picket-fence network acts as a barrier to macroscopic phase separation of lipids.
source: In a recent series of simulations, it was subsequently shown that a picket-fence network also acts as a barrier to macroscopic phase separation of lipids (Ehrig et al., 2011; Fischer and Vink, 2011; Machta et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ehrig et al., 2011; Fischer and Vink, 2011; Machta et al., 2011.

claim: A stable mosaic of Lo and Ld domains is predicted in the presence of a picket-fence network, with a domain structure that strongly correlates to the actin fibers.
source: Instead, a stable mosaic of Lo and Ld domains is predicted, with a domain structure that strongly correlates to the actin fibers.
evidence: This is a prediction from simulations cited in the previous sentence (Ehrig et al., 2011; Fischer and Vink, 2011; Machta et al., 2011).

claim: The mosaic structure of Lo and Ld domains appears at physiological temperatures in the presence of a picket-fence network.
source: Moreover, this mosaic structure already appears at physiological temperatures.
evidence: This is a prediction from simulations cited earlier (Ehrig et al., 2011; Fischer and Vink, 2011; Machta et al., 2011).

claim: The model system consists of a supported lipid bilayer bound to an actin network.
source: To this end, we use an in vitro model system consisting of a supported lipid bilayer bound to an actin network.
evidence: This describes the experimental system used in the study.

claim: The model system enables direct observation of Lo/Ld domain formation in the presence of a lipid bound actin network using superresolution STED microscopy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS).
source: Complementing previous studies (Liu and Fletcher, 2006; Subramaniam et al., 2012; Heinemann et al., 2013; Vogel et al., 2013), our system enables direct observation of Lo/Ld domain formation in the presence of a lipid bound actin network using superresolution STED microscopy (Hell and Wichmann, 1994; Hell, 2007) and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) (Magde et al., 1972; Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the techniques used (Hell and Wichmann, 1994; Hell, 2007; Magde et al., 1972; Kim et al., 2007) and previous studies (Liu and Fletcher, 2006; Subramaniam et al., 2012; Heinemann et al., 2013; Vogel et al., 2013).

claim: The pinning effect of the actin network is dramatically enhanced by coupling of the local membrane curvature to the membrane composition.
source: Computer simulations of this extended model show that the pinning effect of the actin network is dramatically enhanced by such a coupling.
evidence: This is a finding from the computer simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: Even a low density of pinning sites can induce significant structuring of lipids and proteins in the plasma membrane.
source: These results imply that even a low density of pinning sites can induce significant structuring of lipids and proteins in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The model system is a lipid mixture of unsaturated DOPC, saturated DPPC, and cholesterol.
source: Our model system is a lipid mixture of unsaturated DOPC, saturated DPPC, and cholesterol.
evidence: This describes the composition of the experimental model system.

claim: Ternary mixtures of DOPC, DPPC, and cholesterol are routinely used to approximate the complex lipid composition of the eukaryotic plasma membrane.
source: Such ternary mixtures are routinely used to approximate the complex lipid composition of the eukaryotic plasma membrane (Dimova et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dimova et al., 2006.

claim: The phase diagram for the DOPC/DPPC/cholesterol system in the absence of actin is well known.
source: The phase diagram for this system in the absence of actin is well known (Veatch and Keller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Veatch and Keller, 2003.

claim: For a large range of compositions, the DOPC/DPPC/cholesterol system reveals macroscopic Lo/Ld phase coexistence below the transition temperature Tc, while above Tc they are homogenously mixed.
source: For a large range of compositions this system reveals macroscopic Lo/Ld phase coexistence below the transition temperature Tc, while above Tc they are homogenously mixed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the phase behavior of this lipid system.

claim: Domains grow largest in unsupported membranes.
source: Domains grow largest in unsupported membranes (Honigmann et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Honigmann et al., 2010.

claim: Domains are smaller in Mica supported membranes.
source: they are smaller in Mica supported membranes (Jensen et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2007.

claim: Domains are below the diffraction limit on glass-supported membranes.
source: and are below the diffraction limit on glass-supported membranes (Honigmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Honigmann et al., 2013.

claim: The composition ratio used in the present work is (DOPC:DPPC:cholesterol) = (35:35:30) mol%, including 1 mol% of a biotinylated lipid (DOPE-biotin).
source: In the present work, we choose a composition ratio of (DOPC:DPPC:cholesterol) = (35:35:30) mol%, including 1 mol% of a biotinylated lipid (DOPE-biotin) to eventually connect the membrane to an actin network.
evidence: This describes the specific composition used in the experiments.

claim: Upon cooling, there is a well-defined temperature at which Lo/Ld domains became visible in the absence of actin.
source: Visual inspection of images revealed that, upon cooling, there is a well-defined temperature at which Lo/Ld domains became visible (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The phase transition temperature is around Tc ≈ 28°C.
source: This temperature is around Tc ≈ 28°C and thus marks the transition between the mixed one-phase state at high temperature, and the low-temperature two-phase coexistence state.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The phase transition temperature is close but slightly decreased compared to the reported value for lipid vesicles made of the same mixture (Tc ≈ 30°C).
source: This phase transition temperature is close but slightly decreased compared to the reported value for lipid vesicles made of the same mixture (Tc ≈ 30°C [Veatch et al., 2004]).
evidence: This compares the measured value to a cited reference (Veatch et al., 2004).

claim: At Tc, domains were constantly forming and re-forming, implying that the line tension is small, and so the transition is close to critical.
source: At Tc, domains were constantly forming and re-forming, implying that the line tension is small, and so the transition is close to critical.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed behavior of domains at Tc.

claim: In the one-phase region, U1 = π/2, whereas for a two-phase system U1 = 1.
source: In the one-phase region, U1 = π/2, whereas for a two-phase system U1 = 1 (Binder, 1981; Fischer and Vink, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Binder, 1981 and Fischer and Vink, 2011.

claim: U1 markedly dropped toward unity below Tc.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, U1 markedly dropped toward unity below Tc.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Once the membrane enters the two-phase region, domains were seen to coarsen within a couple of minutes.
source: Once the membrane enters the two-phase region, domains were seen to coarsen within a couple of minutes.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: R increased rapidly at Tc, from <75 nm to >200 nm, and continued to grow into the near micrometer range as the temperature was lowered further.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, R increased rapidly at Tc, from <75 nm to >200 nm, and continued to grow into the near micrometer range as the temperature was lowered further.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The findings are consistent with atomic force microscopy experiments, where the transition was shown to be continuous.
source: These findings are consistent with atomic force microscopy experiments (Connell et al., 2013), where the transition was shown to be continuous as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Connell et al., 2013.

claim: The observation that the domains do not fully coalesce at low temperature can be attributed to the interaction of the membrane with the mica support.
source: The observation that the domains do not fully coalesce at low temperature (as opposed to free-standing membranes) can be attributed to the interaction of the membrane with the mica support (Jensen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2007.

claim: With actin, domains already appeared at T ≈ 37°C.
source: Visual inspection of images (Figure 1B) revealed that, with actin, domains already appeared at T ≈ 37°C.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the presence of actin, a partitioning of the membrane into compartments of Lo-enriched domains, separated by 'channels' of Ld-enriched domains was observed.
source: We observed a partitioning of the membrane into compartments of Lo-enriched domains, separated by 'channels' of Ld-enriched domains.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The Ld channels were clearly correlated to the actin fibers.
source: These channels were clearly correlated to the actin fibers (middle row), as shown in the overlay (lower row).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PCC is largest at low temperature, implying that the correlation between Ld domains and actin is strongest there.
source: We observed that PCC is largest at low temperature, implying that the correlation between Ld domains and actin is strongest there (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PCC remains finite at high temperatures also, with a significant correlation up to the highest accessible temperatures of T = 37°C.
source: However, PCC remains finite at high temperatures also, with a significant correlation up to our highest accessible temperatures of T = 37°C, which is a stunning 9°C above Tc of the actin-free membrane.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: For T > 28°C, the decrease of PCC is approximately linear.
source: For T > 28°C, the decrease of PCC is approximately linear.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The decrease in PCC was caused by an increasingly even partitioning of the Ld-marker, and not by a redistribution of Ld domains away from the actin fibers.
source: This decrease was caused by an increasingly even partitioning of the Ld-marker, and not by a redistribution of Ld domains away from the actin fibers (as follows from Figure 1B, where correlated domains remain clearly visible at T = 37°C).
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the presence of actin, there is no phase transition associated with the formation of the domain structure.
source: In contrast to the actin-free case, our data suggest that there is no phase transition associated with the formation of the domain structure: Neither the cumulant nor the domain size revealed any pronounced temperature dependence (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: In the presence of actin, the average domain size was significantly smaller, R ≈ 90 nm at most, and no coarsening was observed.
source: Furthermore, in the presence of actin, the average domain size was significantly smaller, R ≈ 90 nm at most, and no coarsening was observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The phase transition of the actin-free membrane is effectively eliminated by the actin network.
source: Our conclusion is that the phase transition of the actin-free membrane is effectively eliminated by the actin network, in line with theoretical expectations (Fischer and Vink, 2011; Machta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to Fischer and Vink, 2011 and Machta et al., 2011.

claim: In a single component bilayer (DOPC) bound to actin, no domains were induced by the actin.
source: As control experiment, we also considered a single component bilayer (DOPC) bound to actin. In this case, no domains were induced by the actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The actin-correlated phases were not induced by the green-fluorescent phalloidin.
source: Additionally, we excluded the possibility that the actin-correlated phases were induced by the green-fluorescent phalloidin. To this end, we stained the membrane with the Ld-marker (red) and the Lo marker (green) but not the actin itself. The result was a comparable structure as observed in Figure 1B, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the single component membrane, the autocorrelation analysis revealed no significant differences in mobility between areas with actin and without.
source: For the single component membrane, the autocorrelation analysis revealed no significant differences in mobility between areas with actin and without.
evidence: This is an observation from the FCS analysis.

claim: For the single component membrane, the amplitude and correlation time of the pair-correlation revealed no clear directional dependence.
source: For the single component membrane, the amplitude and correlation time revealed no clear directional dependence.
evidence: This is an observation from the pair-correlation analysis.

claim: The average correlation time across the circle was τ ≈ 30 ms for the single component membrane, indicating that the pinning of the actin filament imposed no significant diffusion barrier for lipids.
source: The average correlation time across the circle was τ ≈ 30 ms, indicating that the pinning of the actin filament imposed no significant diffusion barrier for lipids.
evidence: This is an observation and inference from the pair-correlation analysis.

claim: Point FCS measurements on single component membranes in the presence of increasing actin densities showed that lateral diffusion was remarkably insensitive to the presence of actin.
source: These results are in agreement with point FCS measurements on single component membranes in the presence of increasing actin densities, which are reported in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E. Also here, the lateral diffusion was remarkably insensitive to the presence of actin.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: In the ternary system, a pronounced directional dependence of lipid diffusion was observed.
source: In contrast to the single component membrane, a pronounced directional dependence of lipid diffusion was observed in the ternary system.
evidence: This is an observation from the FCS analysis.

claim: The intensity distribution of the Ld-marker showed a slight increase at the position of the actin fiber, indicating a stabilized Ld phase along the actin fiber.
source: The intensity distribution of the Ld-marker showed a slight increase at the position of the actin fiber (upper panel Figure 2C), indicating a stabilized Ld phase along the actin fiber.
evidence: This is an observation and inference from the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The pair-correlation function revealed strong peaks at 0 and 180° (i.e., along the actin filament) at delay times τ ≈ 30–50 ms.
source: While the autocorrelation analysis along the scan trajectory indicated no clear heterogeneities (lower panel Figure 2C), the pair-correlation function revealed strong peaks at 0 and 180° (i.e., along the actin filament) at delay times τ ≈ 30–50 ms (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the direction perpendicular to the actin fiber, a much weaker amplitude was observed, with the peak shifted to longer times τ > 50ms.
source: In the direction perpendicular to the actin fiber, a much weaker amplitude was observed, with the peak shifted to longer times τ > 50ms.
evidence: This is an observation from the pair-correlation analysis.

claim: The actin stabilized Ld domains favored the diffusion of the Ld marker within the domain (and thus along the actin fiber), while restricting diffusion across domain boundaries.
source: This indicates that the actin stabilized Ld domains favored the diffusion of the Ld marker within the domain (and thus along the actin fiber), while restricting diffusion across domain boundaries.
evidence: This is an inference from the pair-correlation analysis results.

claim: The findings strikingly confirm the simulation prediction of Machta et al. (2011), where lipid domains stabilized by actin pinning were also found to 'compartmentalize' lipid diffusion.
source: These findings strikingly confirm the simulation prediction of Machta et al. (2011), where lipid domains stabilized by actin pinning were also found to 'compartmentalize' lipid diffusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Machta et al. (2011) and the experimental data.

claim: DOPE-biotin partitions strongly into the Ld phase (Lo% = 11 ± 2).
source: DOPE-biotin (i.e., the same as used in the experiment of Figure 1) that partitions strongly into the Ld phase (Lo% = 11 ± 2)
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental procedure outlined in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DSPE-PEG-biotin partitions predominantly in the Lo phase (Lo% = 78 ± 7).
source: DSPE-PEG-biotin that partitions predominantly in the Lo phase (Lo% = 78 ± 7)
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental procedure outlined in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DPPE-biotin partitions almost equally in both phases but with a small preference toward the Lo phase (Lo% = 59 ± 5).
source: and DPPE-biotin that partitions almost equally in both phases (but with a small preference toward the Lo phase, Lo% = 59 ± 5).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental procedure outlined in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pinning of the Ld-preferring lipid DOPE-biotin resulted in the formation of Ld domains along the actin fibers, with a positive Pearson coefficient PCC = 0.55 ± 0.02.
source: In Figure 3A, we show confocal images of the domain structure for the Ld-preferring pinning lipid DOPE-biotin. The figure confirms the previous experiment of Figure 1B: We again observe the formation of Ld domains along the actin fibers, as expressed by a positive Pearson coefficient PCC = 0.55 ± 0.02.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Pinning of the Lo-preferring lipid DSPE-PEG-biotin induced an 'inverted' domain structure, yielding a negative PCC = −0.37 ± 0.04.
source: Pinning of the Lo-preferring lipid DSPE-PEG-biotin induced an 'inverted' domain structure, yielding a negative PCC = −0.37 ± 0.04 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The binding of actin to DPPE-biotin did not result in a strong localization of lipid domains along the fibers, as manifested by a small 'but positive' PCC = 0.07 ± 0.03.
source: The binding of actin to DPPE-biotin did not result in a strong localization of lipid domains along the fibers, as manifested by a small 'but positive' PCC = 0.07 ± 0.03 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The result of Figure 3B is surprising, since DPPE-biotin slightly prefers the Lo phase, and so a 'negative' PCC was expected.
source: The result of Figure 3B is surprising, since DPPE-biotin slightly prefers the Lo phase, and so a 'negative' PCC was expected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expected behavior given the partitioning of DPPE-biotin.

claim: A coupling between membrane composition and curvature can bring about the effect observed in Figure 3B.
source: Notwithstanding that several mechanisms could be responsible for this (e.g., streptavidin binding to biotinylated lipids may induce lipid disorder by steric or electrostatic interactions with the membrane), it is interesting that a coupling between membrane composition and curvature also brings about this effect.
evidence: This is a speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: The first term describes the membrane elastic properties using the Helfrich form, with bending rigidity κ, and surface tension σ.
source: The first term describes the membrane elastic properties using the Helfrich form (Helfrich, 1973), with bending rigidity κ, and surface tension σ
evidence: This describes the simulation model and is supported by citation to Helfrich, 1973.

claim: The second term describes the phase separation using a conserved order parameter Ising model.
source: the second term describes the phase separation using a conserved order parameter Ising model;
evidence: This describes the simulation model.

claim: The third term couples the phases to the local membrane curvature.
source: the third term couples the phases to the local membrane curvature.
evidence: This describes the simulation model.

claim: For g = 0, the model reduces to the one of Machta et al. (2011).
source: For g = 0 our model reduces to the one of Machta et al. (2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between the current model and a previous model.

claim: For g > 0, regions of positive curvature favor unsaturated lipids, that is Ld domains.
source: The latter is defined such that, for g > 0, regions of positive curvature favor unsaturated lipids, that is Ld domains.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the simulation model.

claim: At g ≈ 20, the PCC changes sign and crosses the experimental value for DPPE-biotin pinning sites.
source: The key observation is that, at g ≈ 20, the PCC changes sign and crosses the experimental value.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: By artificially broadening the simulation images, lower values g ∼ 10 were obtained.
source: We emphasize that the simulation data were not corrected for the optical point spread function (PSF) of the experiment; by artificially broadening the simulation images, lower values g ∼ 10 were obtained, precluding a precise determination.
evidence: This is a statement about the simulation analysis.

claim: The value of g, where the PCC changes sign also depends on the pinning density: by increasing ρp, also g must increase to result in a positive PCC.
source: In addition, the value of g, where the PCC changes sign also depends on the pinning density: by increasing ρp, also g must increase to result in a positive PCC.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: The change of sign in the PCC reflects a competition between an energetic attraction between DPPE-biotin and saturated lipids, favoring alignment of Lo domains, vs a curvature-induced repulsion of these lipids away from the actin fibers.
source: In qualitative terms, the change of sign in the PCC reflects a competition between two effects: an energetic attraction between DPPE-biotin and saturated lipids, favoring alignment of Lo domains, vs a curvature-induced repulsion of these lipids away from the actin fibers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: Due to the steric repulsion between the membrane and the actin fibers, the preferred curvature around the fibers is positive on average, thereby favoring Ld domains.
source: Due to the steric repulsion between the membrane and the actin fibers, the preferred curvature around the fibers is positive on average, thereby favoring Ld domains.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation model.

claim: At large g, the curvature effect dominates, yielding a positive Pearson coefficient.
source: At large g, the latter effect dominates, yielding a positive Pearson coefficient.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The simulation snapshot corresponding to g = 20 and ρp = 0.1/nm shows a structure of small domains, in agreement with the experiment of Figure 3B.
source: In Figure 4E, we show a typical snapshot corresponding to g = 20 and ρp = 0.1/nm. In agreement with the experiment of Figure 3B, we observe a structure of small domains.
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation and experimental results.

claim: By using g = 0, the domains grow to be much larger, contradicting the experimental observations.
source: In contrast, by using g = 0, the domains grow to be much larger (Figure 4B), contradicting the experimental observations.
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation and experimental results.

claim: In the presence of curvature coupling, the pinning density required to induce domain alignment along the actin fibers can be much smaller.
source: Our model also predicts that, in the presence of curvature coupling, the pinning density required to induce domain alignment along the actin fibers can be much smaller.
evidence: This is a prediction from the simulation model.

claim: Previous simulations corresponding to g = 0 required rather large pinning densities, ρp ∼ 0.2 − 1.25/nm, in order to achieve domain alignment.
source: Previous simulations corresponding to g = 0 (Ehrig et al., 2011; Machta et al., 2011) required rather large pinning densities, ρp ∼ 0.2 − 1.25/nm, in order to achieve this.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ehrig et al., 2011 and Machta et al., 2011.

claim: To reproduce the experimentally observed domain structure at low pinning densities, curvature coupling is essential.
source: To reproduce the experimentally observed domain structure (Figure 3A) at low pinning densities, curvature coupling is thus essential.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing simulation and experimental results.

claim: In Figure 4D, the average Ld domain size Rsim ≈ 40 nm, which is somewhat below Rexp ≈ 90 nm of the experiment.
source: In Figure 4D, the average Ld domain size Rsim ≈ 40 nm, which is somewhat below Rexp ≈ 90 nm of the experiment (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation and experimental results.

claim: The experimental value likely presents an upper-bound, due to broadening by the PSF.
source: Note, however, that the experimental value likely presents an upper-bound, due to broadening by the PSF.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental measurement.

claim: Curvature coupling is required to reproduce the inverted domain structure observed with DSPE-PEG-biotin pinning sites.
source: The case of DSPE-PEG-biotin pinning sites (Lo% = 78 ± 7) is considered in Figure 4C,F. Again, curvature coupling is required to reproduce the (now inverted) domain structure of the experiment (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing simulation and experimental results.

claim: In the presence of curvature coupling, the length scale over which the effect of a pinning site propagates is enhanced dramatically.
source: In the presence of curvature coupling, the length scale over which the effect of a pinning site propagates is thus enhanced dramatically.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The bending rigidity and the surface tension define a length ξh = (κ/σ)1/2, which sets the scale over which the membrane height deformations propagate (for the model parameters ξh ∼ 100 nm).
source: This is due to the elastic properties of the membrane: the bending rigidity and the surface tension define a length ξh = (κ/σ)1/2 (Schick, 2012), which sets the scale over which the membrane height deformations propagate (for our model parameters ξh ∼ 100 nm).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schick, 2012 and the simulation model parameters.

claim: When g > 0, the length scale couples to the composition, in which case a reduced pinning density already suffices to induce domain alignment.
source: When g > 0, this scale couples to the composition, in which case a reduced pinning density already suffices to induce domain alignment.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation model.

claim: ξh is essentially independent of temperature, and so it is not necessary for the membrane to be close to a critical point.
source: We emphasize that ξh is essentially independent of temperature, and so it is not necessary for the membrane to be close to a critical point.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation model.

claim: Ld domains (magenta) reveal positive curvature on average, while for Lo domains (black) the curvature is on average negative.
source: These profiles qualitatively illustrate the curvature coupling effect: Ld domains (magenta) reveal positive curvature on average, while for Lo domains (black) the curvature is on average negative.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation height profiles shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the absence of coupling to actin and g = 0, the typical root-mean-square height fluctuation is h ≈ 3.6 nm.
source: In the absence of coupling to actin and g = 0, the typical root-mean-square height fluctuation is h ≈ 3.6 nm.
evidence: This is a measurement from the simulation.

claim: In the presence of actin and curvature coupling, height fluctuations are significantly reduced to h ≈ 2nm, which is very close to the value reported in Speck et al. (2010).
source: In the presence of actin and curvature coupling, these fluctuations are significantly reduced to h ≈ 2nm, which is very close to the value reported in Speck et al. (2010).
evidence: This is a measurement from the simulation and is supported by citation to Speck et al. (2010).

claim: The application of the model system to a single component liquid-disordered membrane shows that actin has only a minor influence on the lateral distribution and dynamics of lipids.
source: The application of our model system to a single component liquid-disordered membrane shows that actin has only a minor influence on the lateral distribution and dynamics of lipids (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, as well as Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2A,B.

claim: Under the same conditions using a ternary membrane, the effects of actin are dramatic.
source: In contrast, under the same conditions using a ternary membrane, the effects are dramatic.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The experiments confirm the absence of macroscopic phase separation in the presence of actin, in agreement with earlier simulation predictions.
source: In agreement with these simulations, our experiments confirm the absence of macroscopic phase separation in the presence of actin.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results and is supported by citations to earlier simulations (Ehrig et al., 2011; Fischer and Vink, 2011; Machta et al., 2011).

claim: The experiments revealed the alignment of Ld domains along the actin fibers, leading to a channel-like domain structure very similar to structures observed in simulations.
source: Additionally, our experiments revealed the alignment of Ld domains along the actin fibers, leading to a channel-like domain structure very similar to structures observed in simulations (Ehrig et al., 2011; Fischer and Vink, 2011; Machta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results and is supported by citations to simulations (Ehrig et al., 2011; Fischer and Vink, 2011; Machta et al., 2011).

claim: In agreement with the simulations of Machta et al. (2011), the enhanced diffusion of unsaturated lipids along the Ld channels, and the hindered diffusion of these lipids in directions perpendicular, was confirmed.
source: Finally, in agreement with the simulations of Machta et al. (2011), the enhanced diffusion of unsaturated lipids along the Ld channels, and the hindered diffusion of these lipids in directions perpendicular, was confirmed.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results and is supported by citation to Machta et al. (2011).

claim: Relatively simple simulation models are capable to capture key essentials of lateral membrane organization and dynamics.
source: These findings demonstrate that relatively simple simulation models are capable to capture key essentials of lateral membrane organization and dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the agreement between simulations and experiments.

claim: By using pinning sites that weakly attract the Lo phase, the experiments uncover phenomena that cannot be explained using previous simulation models.
source: However, by using pinning sites that weakly attract the Lo phase, our experiments also uncover phenomena that cannot be explained using these simulation models.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: For pinning sites that weakly attract the Lo phase, one still observes alignment of Ld domains along the actin fibers, albeit weak.
source: The paradox is that, for the latter type of pinning site, one still observes alignment of Ld domains along the actin fibers, albeit weak.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental results.

claim: There must be additional mechanisms at play—beyond the level of the pinning-lipid energetic interaction—playing a role in the lateral organization of the membrane.
source: This indicates that there must be additional mechanisms at play—beyond the level of the pinning-lipid energetic interaction—playing a role in the lateral organization of the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: A simulation model that incorporates local membrane curvature and a coupling of the latter to the lipid composition is able to reproduce the experimentally observed alignment of Ld domains, even when the pinning sites themselves energetically favor the Lo phase.
source: As possible candidate for such a mechanism, we considered the local membrane curvature, and a coupling of the latter to the lipid composition (Schick, 2012). A simulation model that incorporates these ingredients is able to reproduce the experimentally observed alignment of Ld domains, even when the pinning sites themselves energetically favor the Lo phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results and is supported by citation to Schick, 2012.

claim: The actin network locally induces regions with non-zero average curvature.
source: The physical explanation is that the actin network locally induces regions with non-zero average curvature.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation model.

claim: The coupling of the curvature to the composition causes regions with non-zero average curvature to prefer certain types of lipids.
source: The coupling of the curvature to the composition then causes these regions to prefer certain types of lipids.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation model.

claim: Provided the coupling is strong enough, it can overcome the pinning-lipid energetic interaction.
source: Provided the coupling is strong enough, it can overcome the pinning-lipid energetic interaction, which is how we interpret the experimental result.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental and simulation results.

claim: Curvature coupling is not the only conceivable mechanism that could account for the experimental findings.
source: We emphasize once more that curvature coupling is not the only conceivable mechanism that could account for our experimental findings.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging alternative explanations.

claim: A recent experimental study of membrane phase separation using intermembrane junctions uncovered a very pronounced curvature coupling.
source: However, a recent experimental study (Kaizuka and Groves, 2010) of membrane phase separation using intermembrane junctions did uncover a very pronounced curvature coupling, making this a likely candidate.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaizuka and Groves, 2010.

claim: The type of lipid domain selected to be stabilized depends sensitively on the properties of the pinning species.
source: Our experiments show that the type of lipid domain selected to be stabilized depends sensitively on the properties of the pinning species.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: A similar phenomenon, albeit on a larger scale, was observed by crosslinking GM1 with cholera toxin B.
source: A similar phenomenon, albeit on a larger scale, was observed by crosslinking GM1 with cholera toxin B (Hammond et al., 2005; Lingwood et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hammond et al., 2005 and Lingwood et al., 2008.

claim: Since the stabilized phase is determined by the properties of the pinning species, cells could locally sort their membrane components in this way.
source: Since the stabilized phase is determined by the properties of the pinning species, cells could locally sort their membrane components in this way.
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological implications.

claim: This sorting mechanism persists to physiological temperatures, that is above the temperature of phase separation.
source: Moreover, this sorting mechanism persists to physiological temperatures, that is above the temperature of phase separation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The pinning sites would naturally prevent the plasma membrane from phase separating at low temperatures.
source: At the same time, the pinning sites would naturally prevent the plasma membrane from phase separating at low temperatures.
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological implications.

claim: In the presence of curvature coupling, the effects of pinning sites are enhanced.
source: In the presence of curvature coupling, these effects are enhanced.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The proposed curvature effect in the experiments was likely limited by the Mica support.
source: We note that the proposed curvature effect in our experiments was likely limited by the Mica support.
evidence: This is a speculation about the experimental system.

claim: Since the energy cost of lipid extraction far exceeds that of membrane de-adhesion from the support, some curvature effect is still expected.
source: However, since the energy cost of lipid extraction far exceeds that of membrane de-adhesion from the support (Helm et al., 1991; Lipowsky and Seifert, 1991), we still expect some effect.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Helm et al., 1991 and Lipowsky and Seifert, 1991.

claim: In free-standing membranes, or in cell membranes, the curvature-coupling is anticipated to be stronger.
source: In free-standing membranes, or in cell membranes, the curvature-coupling is anticipated to be stronger.
evidence: This is a speculation about other membrane systems.

claim: The recent findings of Kaizuka and Groves (2010) seem to support the view that curvature-coupling is stronger in free-standing membranes.
source: The recent findings of Kaizuka and Groves (2010) seem to support this view.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaizuka and Groves (2010).
